blocks.text: Deploying a fine-tuned model well requires pulling together decisions from across the Inference and Serving and Production Fine-Tuning modules, both covered earlier in this course, into a coherent deployment plan, this topic walks through that full sequence of decisions as a single practical reference.

The deployment path chosen depends heavily on decisions made during training, particularly whether an adapter was merged or kept loaded, making it worth planning deployment before training even finishes rather than treating it as an afterthought.

The full deployment path connects several stages covered separately in earlier topics, exporting the trained model into a deployable format, covered in the Model Export topic, loading it into a chosen serving framework, and exposing it as a production endpoint that application code actually calls.

The adapter merging versus loading decision, covered in earlier topics, should be made based on the actual deployment need, merge for a single fixed-behavior deployment with zero runtime overhead, keep loaded if the deployment needs to serve multiple task-specific behaviors from a shared base model, this decision shapes everything downstream.

The four serving frameworks covered in the earlier Inference and Serving module each fit a different scenario, vLLM for general high-throughput GPU serving, Ollama for local or consumer hardware, TensorRT-LLM when maximum hardware-specific performance justifies the added complexity, and TGI for teams already deep in the Hugging Face ecosystem.

blocks.text: Applying the quantization techniques covered in an earlier module specifically at export time, separate from any quantization used during QLoRA training, can further shrink the deployed model and improve serving throughput, worth evaluating as a deployment-time optimization even if training itself used full precision.

# Export merged model, then quantize specifically for serving
merged_model.save_pretrained("./merged")
# followed by a serving-specific quantization pass, e.g. AWQ or GPTQ

blocks.text: 5. Rolling Out Gradually Rather Than All at Once

blocks.alt: Rolling Out Gradually Rather Than All at Once

blocks.text: Connecting to the A/B testing and champion-challenger pattern covered in earlier topics, rolling a newly deployed model out gradually, a small percentage of traffic first, or shadow deployment where it processes real traffic without its output being shown to users, catches problems before they affect the full user base.

blocks.title: This is the same safety principle covered in the retraining pipelines topic, applied to first deployment
blocks.content: Whether it is a first deployment or a retrained replacement model, the champion-challenger and gradual rollout principles covered in the earlier Retraining Pipelines topic apply equally, never fully trust a new model with all production traffic immediately.

blocks.text: 6. Connecting Deployment to Monitoring and Retraining

blocks.alt: Connecting Deployment to Monitoring and Retraining

blocks.text: A deployed model is not a finished, static artifact, the monitoring approach covered in an earlier topic should feed directly into the retraining pipeline covered in another earlier topic, closing the loop from deployment back through to detecting when the model needs to be updated again.

Before committing to a full production launch, load testing the chosen serving framework and hardware configuration against expected traffic volume confirms the deployment can actually handle real load, catching capacity issues in a controlled test rather than during an actual traffic spike.

The cost optimization techniques covered in an earlier topic, right-sizing hardware, choosing an appropriate quantization level, batching strategy, all directly affect ongoing serving cost, worth revisiting specifically at deployment time rather than assuming training-time decisions automatically translate into an optimal serving configuration.

Pulling this topic together into a checklist, decide merge versus load, choose a serving framework matching the actual use case, consider serving-time quantization, plan a gradual rollout rather than a full immediate launch, connect monitoring to the retraining pipeline, and load test before committing to production traffic.

A team finishing a QLoRA fine-tuning run for a customer-facing chat application decides to keep their adapter loaded rather than merged, since they plan to serve several customer-specific adapters from one shared base model, they choose vLLM for its native multi-adapter serving support and high-throughput GPU serving.

Before full launch, they load test the deployment against expected peak traffic, then roll out to five percent of production traffic first, watching monitoring metrics closely before gradually increasing to full traffic, with their monitoring pipeline already connected to trigger a retraining review if quality metrics drop below a defined threshold.

items: Deciding merge versus load as an afterthought after training completes rather than planning it upfront
Choosing a serving framework based on popularity rather than which specific framework fits the actual deployment scenario
Launching a new model directly to full production traffic without a gradual rollout or load testing first
Treating deployment as the final step rather than connecting it to ongoing monitoring and retraining

blocks.text: For a fine-tuned model deployment scenario you are familiar with or could imagine, walk through the checklist covered in this topic, merge versus load decision, framework choice, rollout strategy, and monitoring connection, and justify each choice based on the specific scenario requirements.

Deploying a fine-tuned model well means planning the merge versus load decision, serving framework choice, and rollout strategy together as one coherent pipeline rather than a single afterthought step, connecting deployment directly to the monitoring and retraining pipeline covered in earlier topics so that a deployed model remains a starting point for continued improvement rather than a static, finished artifact.
